pathway.title: Web Development
pathway.description: A progressive pathway for planning, building, testing, securing and operating modern websites and web applications.

course.title: Web Development — Beginner
course.dependencies: HTML5, CSS and browser JavaScript; no framework required.
course.short_description: Build accessible, responsive websites from HTML foundations through CSS and JavaScript fundamentals.
course.prerequisites: Basic computer literacy; no prior programming experience is required.
learning_outcomes: Structure meaningful pages with semantic HTML.
Style responsive layouts with CSS, typography and accessible visual states.
Use JavaScript fundamentals and DOM events to add useful interactions.
Publish and evaluate a small accessible website.

lesson.title: How the web works and document structure
objectives: Explain the core ideas behind how the web works and document structure.
Apply how the web works and document structure in a small, testable web-development task.
Evaluate accessibility, security or maintainability implications relevant to how the web works and document structure.

blocks.title: Concepts and engineering context
blocks.body:
A web page is not merely a picture on a screen: it is a structured document interpreted by a browser. HTML describes meaning and relationships, CSS controls presentation and layout, and JavaScript adds behavior. Browsers request resources using HTTP, parse HTML into a document tree, discover stylesheets and scripts, calculate layout, paint pixels and respond to user input. These stages are related but distinct. Good structure starts with a clear purpose for each page and semantic elements that communicate meaning to browsers, assistive technologies and other developers. Semantic markup often provides useful behavior without custom code: links navigate, buttons perform actions, labels identify form controls, and headings create an outline. A robust page should still communicate its core information when styling is unavailable. Build progressively: create meaningful HTML first, add CSS for visual hierarchy and responsive layout, then add JavaScript only where interaction is needed. Validate the result at narrow and wide viewport sizes, with keyboard navigation, and with content that is longer or shorter than the sample. This approach produces pages that are easier to understand, test and maintain.

In this lesson, focus specifically on how the web works and document structure. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

blocks.title: A small executable example
blocks.expected_output: Learning Web Development: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
blocks.explanation: This small JavaScript example models data and transforms it into a readable summary. It runs in Node.js and demonstrates the language behavior used in browser scripts; the surrounding lesson explains how the same idea fits into web architecture.

Explain one trade-off in your design.
success_checks: The result meets the stated behavior and has a clear structure.

blocks.body:
A web page is not merely a picture on a screen: it is a structured document interpreted by a browser. HTML describes meaning and relationships, CSS controls presentation and layout, and JavaScript adds behavior. Browsers request resources using HTTP, parse HTML into a document tree, discover stylesheets and scripts, calculate layout, paint pixels and respond to user input. These stages are related but distinct. Good structure starts with a clear purpose for each page and semantic elements that communicate meaning to browsers, assistive technologies and other developers. Semantic markup often provides useful behavior without custom code: links navigate, buttons perform actions, labels identify form controls, and headings create an outline. A robust page should still communicate its core information when styling is unavailable. Build progressively: create meaningful HTML first, add CSS for visual hierarchy and responsive layout, then add JavaScript only where interaction is needed. Validate the result at narrow and wide viewport sizes, with keyboard navigation, and with content that is longer or shorter than the sample. This approach produces pages that are easier to understand, test and maintain.

In this lesson, focus specifically on dom selection, events and validation. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

practical_project.title: Web Development — Beginner Capstone
practical_project.purpose: Design and build a responsive multi-page informational website that demonstrates the course outcomes.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional data and test accounts only; do not connect to Marian production systems or real learner records.
Do not put credentials, API secrets or private keys in browser code.
A learning prototype is not a security certification or production approval.
requirements: Write a short user and feature brief with acceptance criteria.
Use semantic HTML, responsive CSS and a clear component or page structure.
Implement the required interactions and validate user input.
Handle empty, loading, success and error states where data is asynchronous.
Include keyboard and accessibility checks appropriate to the interface.
Add automated tests for important behavior and document setup and limitations.
suggested_steps: Define users, scope, acceptance criteria and a simple architecture diagram.
Build the semantic structure and responsive visual system.
Implement behavior and data boundaries in small increments.
Test normal, boundary, accessibility and failure cases.
Review performance, security and maintainability appropriate to the level.
Document setup, screenshots, decisions and known limitations.
success_checks: The application satisfies its stated acceptance criteria.
The interface works at mobile and desktop widths.
Core tasks are possible using a keyboard.
Important normal and failure cases are tested.
The README explains setup, architecture and limitations.

rubric.look_for: Clear scope, coherent structure and justified design decisions.
Correct behavior, readable code and maintainable organization.
Semantic structure, keyboard use, contrast and adaptable layout.
Relevant automated and manual tests, including boundary cases.
Reproducible setup, diagrams, trade-offs and honest limitations.
